mcqs.question: Which of the following is a common mistake when using a ruler to measure the length of an object?

options.A: Aligning the zero mark of the ruler with one end of the object and reading the measurement at the other end.
options.B: Placing the ruler’s edge directly on the object and reading the measurement at the far end.
options.C: Starting the measurement from the 1 cm mark instead of the 0 cm mark.
options.D: Using a ruler that is broken or has missing markings.

mcqs.answer: Starting the measurement from the 1 cm mark instead of the 0 cm mark.
mcqs.explanation: The zero mark on a ruler indicates the true starting point. Beginning at the 1 cm mark adds an extra 1 cm to every measurement, leading to systematic over‑measurement. Options A and B describe correct practices, while D is a problem with the tool, not a typical misconception.

mcqs.question: A student places the 0 cm mark of a ruler at the far end of a pencil and then reads the measurement at the near end. How will this affect the recorded length?

options.A: The length will be measured correctly.
options.D: The ruler will give a negative value.

mcqs.explanation: When the zero mark is placed at the far end, the reading taken at the near end represents only the portion of the pencil that lies before the zero point, which is shorter than the actual length. Hence the measurement is smaller than the true length. Option B is the opposite error, and A and D are incorrect for this setup.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly compares how you read measurements on a metric ruler and an imperial ruler?

options.A: Both scales have the smallest division as 1 cm or 1 inch respectively.
options.B: On a metric ruler you read the measurement at the line just before the zero of the next larger unit, while on an imperial ruler you read it at the line just after the zero.
options.C: For both scales you note the number of whole units and then estimate the fraction of the next unit.
options.D: An imperial ruler shows fractions in decimal form, whereas a metric ruler shows fractions as fractions.

mcqs.answer: For both scales you note the number of whole units and then estimate the fraction of the next unit.
mcqs.explanation: Whether the ruler is metric or imperial, the reading process is the same: count the full units (centimetres or inches) and then estimate the part of the next unit based on the smallest marked division. Option A is inaccurate because the smallest division on a metric ruler is often 1 mm, not 1 cm. Option B misstates the reading method, and Option D confuses the way fractions are displayed.

mcqs.question: A ruler has marks at every 1 cm. If an object’s length falls between the 7 cm and 8 cm marks and you estimate it to be 7.4 cm, what is the maximum possible error in your estimate?
mcqs.explanation: The smallest division on the ruler is 1 cm. When estimating between two marks, the greatest uncertainty is half of that division, i.e., ±0.5 cm. Therefore, any estimate between 7 cm and 8 cm could be off by up to half a centimetre. Options A‑C underestimate the possible error.
